source.text: Sutta Nipāta, Khuddaka Nikāya of the Pāli Canon: 6 verses from the Rhinoceros Horn Sutta (Sn 1.3) and all 12 verses of the Maṅgala Sutta (Sn 2.4)
source.translationLicense: English translation and commentary: newly made by Sutra Box from its own Korean version (based on an AI draft, still being reviewed and refined)

sn01.heading: Rhinoceros Horn Sutta · Sn 35
sn01.plain: Laying down the rod toward all living beings, harming not a single one of them, one should not wish even for a child, let alone a companion. Wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.
sn01.commentary: The first verse of the Rhinoceros Horn Sutta. Every verse ends with "wander alone like a rhinoceros horn." The Indian rhinoceros has only one horn, an image of a practitioner who walks alone and firm, not leaning on the herd. It does not mean keeping away from people, but standing on one's own, free of attachment and dependence.

sn02.heading: Rhinoceros Horn Sutta · Sn 36
sn02.plain: From intimacy comes affection, and following affection this suffering arises. Seeing clearly the danger born of affection, wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.
sn02.commentary: It points to where suffering comes from. Meeting people is not bad in itself; it is clinging to those meetings that gives rise to suffering.

sn03.heading: Rhinoceros Horn Sutta · Sn 45–46
sn03.plain: If you find a wise companion fit to walk with, living rightly and steadfast, overcoming all dangers, walk with them gladly and mindfully. But if you do not find a wise companion fit to walk with, living rightly and steadfast, then like a king who leaves behind the kingdom he has conquered, like an elephant roaming alone in the forest, wander alone.
sn03.commentary: These two verses make clear what "wander alone" means. If you meet a good companion, walk together. Only when there is no such companion is it better to go alone than be swept along by bad company.

sn04.heading: Rhinoceros Horn Sutta · Sn 47
sn04.plain: We truly praise the blessing of finding good companions. Companions better than or equal to oneself should be cultivated. Not finding such companions, living on blameless food, wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.
sn04.commentary: The Buddha went so far as to say that good friendship is the whole of the holy life. The teaching to walk alone and the praise of good friends do not conflict.

sn05.heading: Rhinoceros Horn Sutta · Sn 71
sn05.plain: Like a lion not startled by sounds, like the wind not caught in a net, like a lotus not wetted by water, wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.
sn05.commentary: The best-known verse of the Sutta Nipāta. With three images it pictures the practitioner: unshaken by the world's noise (the lion), caught by nothing (the wind), and living in the world yet unstained by it (the lotus).

sn06.heading: Discourse on Blessings · The Question
sn06.plain: Many gods and humans, longing for well-being, have pondered what blessings are. Please tell us the highest blessing.
sn06.commentary: The Discourse on Blessings (Maṅgala Sutta) begins when a deity visits the Buddha at night and asks him this. People thought of lucky days and good omens as blessings, but the Buddha finds true blessing in how we live. It is one of the most chanted discourses in Theravāda Buddhism.

sn07.heading: Discourse on Blessings · Good People and Good Places
sn07.plain: Not associating with fools, associating with the wise, honoring those worthy of honor: this is the highest blessing. Living in a suitable place, having made merit in the past, setting oneself on the right course: this is the highest blessing.
sn07.commentary: The first step of blessing begins with whom we keep company. Good friends, a good environment and a right aim set by oneself are the foundation of life.

sn08.heading: Discourse on Blessings · Learning and Family
sn08.plain: Much learning, skill in a craft, being well trained in discipline, and well-spoken words: this is the highest blessing. Caring for mother and father, supporting spouse and children, and work free of confusion: this is the highest blessing.
sn08.commentary: Learning and skills, right speech, and the everyday tasks of caring for parents and family are all blessings. Practice is not apart from daily life.

sn09.heading: Discourse on Blessings · Giving and Restraint
sn09.plain: Giving, living rightly, supporting relatives, and blameless deeds: this is the highest blessing. Avoiding and abstaining from evil, refraining from intoxicating drink, and not being heedless in good things: this is the highest blessing.
sn09.commentary: Sharing and caring are blessings, and so is the restraint that keeps away from harm. "Not being heedless" was also the Buddha's final exhortation.

sn10.heading: Discourse on Blessings · Humility and Patience
sn10.plain: Respect, humility, contentment, gratitude, and hearing the Dharma at the right time: this is the highest blessing. Patience, being open to advice, seeing monastics, and discussing the Dharma at the right time: this is the highest blessing.
sn10.commentary: Contentment and gratitude, patience and an open ear. A person whose heart is generous and gentle is blessed.

sn11.heading: Discourse on Blessings · An Unshaken Mind
sn11.plain: Ardent practice, a pure life, seeing the noble truths, and realizing nirvana: this is the highest blessing. When touched by the ways of the world, a mind that does not waver, sorrowless, stainless and secure: this is the highest blessing.
sn11.commentary: Blessing finally reaches nirvana and an unshaken mind. The ways of the world are the eight worldly winds: gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain. A mind unshaken by these eight winds is the greatest blessing.

sn12.heading: Discourse on Blessings · Conclusion
sn12.plain: Those who do such things are undefeated everywhere and go everywhere in safety. This is their highest blessing.
sn12.commentary: The closing verse after all thirty-eight blessings have been named. Blessing is not luck that comes from outside; it grows within those who live this way.

khaggavisana.definition: The single horn of the Indian rhinoceros: an image of one who practices alone and steadfast, not leaning on the herd. Some read it as the rhinoceros itself.

mangala.definition: What is auspicious or a blessing. The Buddha called right living itself true blessing, rather than omens or rituals.

four-noble-truths.definition: The four truths of suffering, the cause of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to cessation.

nibbana.definition: Nirvana: the state in which the fires of greed, anger and delusion have gone out; peace in which suffering has completely ended.

eight-worldly.definition: The eight worldly conditions that shake the mind: gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain.
